title: Webb reveals something unexpected in the gas surrounding our galaxy's black hole
excerpt: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has uncovered new clues about the gas surrounding the Milky Way's supermassive black hole and its unusually slow feeding habits.
content:
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has uncovered new clues about the gas surrounding the Milky Way's supermassive black hole and its unusually slow feeding habits.

A black hole is supposed to pull in whatever comes close. Yet the giant one in the middle of our galaxy takes in far less than other big black holes do, and far more slowly.

Now, observations from the James Webb Space Telescope have revealed a possible clue: Gas surrounding the black hole contains about 1.8 times the Sun’s concentration of elements heavier than helium.

Nicole Ford, a Ph.D. student in Daryl Haggard’s group at McGill University, led the work at the university’s Trottier Space Institute.

Her co-authors include astronomers at the Center for Astrophysics run by Harvard and the Smithsonian.

“We know there’s a black hole at the center of our galaxy pulling material into itself, but we see that it’s eating a lot less material than other supermassive black holes, and more slowly,” Ford said.

“Part of understanding why this is happening means looking at the properties of the materials available for it to consume, including gas, dust and the stars orbiting around it.”

Astronomers use the word metals for every element heavier than hydrogen and helium, so carbon, oxygen, iron and gold all count.

Those elements change how fast a cloud of gas can cool, and a cloud that cools can clump and fall toward a black hole. So the mix matters for why this black hole takes in so little.

Sorting the gas by speed

The black hole, called Sagittarius A*, is about 26,000 light-years from Earth. That makes it the closest giant black hole, and the easiest to study.

Webb’s mid-infrared instrument examined gas within about a third of a light-year of the black hole.

Webb split the light finely enough to pick out faint glows from six elements: iron, nickel, sulfur, argon, neon and oxygen.

Each glow also records how fast its gas is moving toward or away from Earth, and that is how the team told the clouds apart.

Each cloud moves at its own speed. The one astronomers call the Bar is barely moving along our line of sight.

A long curved stream called the Northern Arm is heading toward us at about 600,000 miles per hour (270 kilometers per second).

Several small, faint clumps are coming our way at roughly 1.3 million miles per hour (570 kilometers per second). Clumps like these may be the main fuel the black hole eventually takes in.

The data came in April and September 2024, and the longest exposures ran more than 22 hours.

Dead stars likely enriched the gas

Neon and argon were the cleanest elements to measure, because neither one sticks to dust grains. Almost all of it stays in the gas where Webb can see it.

Both came out at about 1.8 times the Sun’s level, with the exact figure ranging from 1.4 to 2.2 times depending on the cloud and the spot measured.

The team adopted 1.8 times solar as the figure for the gas as a whole. Neon and argon are both made inside massive stars and in the explosions that end them. So the researchers think stars that blew up nearby probably supplied the surplus over time.

Earlier studies of the wider galactic center had already measured similar enrichment. What Webb added was the ability to measure it cloud by cloud within a fraction of a light-year of the black hole itself.

Sulfur, iron and nickel were harder. Some of their atoms get locked inside dust grains, and some exist in forms the telescope could not detect, so the team had to estimate the missing share.

The totals for those three elements ranged from a little below the Sun’s level to above it, depending on the cloud.

Shocks likely broke up the dust

Iron also pointed to what has happened to the dust. In dusty parts of the galactic center, usually only 5% to 10% of the iron is free in the gas, and the rest is locked up in grains.

Around the black hole, the team found most of the iron in the gas instead.

Dust grains don’t release their iron on their own. Shocks, the fast collisions between streams of gas, are good at breaking grains apart.

The researchers concluded that the dust in this region has been strongly processed, which fits shock damage.

Nickel fit the same picture. The fast-moving clumps and the Northern Arm held noticeably more nickel in their gas than the Bar did, which fits more extensive shock damage in the two faster features.

The clumps and the Northern Arm were also the most strongly ionized, meaning more of their atoms had lost electrons.

Most of that ionizing light can be explained by the roughly 30 hot, massive Wolf-Rayet stars that orbit near the black hole.

The black hole’s own feeding is too faint to add much. The fast clumps may also be lit partly by shocks they set off as they push through the surrounding gas.

Gas and stars match

Stars orbiting near Sagittarius A* had been measured before, and most of them hold one to two times the Sun’s share of metals.

The Wolf-Rayet stars are thought to have formed from gas in the same range. The gas Webb measured falls in that range too.

Such a match suggests the gas and the stars came from the same material, the team wrote. It fits a picture in which a dense disk of gas formed around the black hole and then collapsed into the stars seen there today.

The alternative, with the stars forming farther out and moving in, fits less well.

Metal content also matters for why the black hole takes in so little.

One recent set of simulations found that gas with about three times the Sun’s metals may mark a threshold for cooling efficiently into a disk that feeds the black hole.

The gas Webb measured falls below that line.

The mystery isn’t solved yet

Oxygen glowed too faintly for a reliable measurement. The fast clumps’ density had to be borrowed from an earlier estimate for one of them, a well-studied clump named X7.

If the clumps are thinner than assumed, their ionization reads differently.

The team can’t yet say whether the fast clumps are lit mainly by the Wolf-Rayet stars or by their own shocks.

Telling those apart would take sharper measurements of light from atoms that need the most energy to ionize, such as oxygen missing three electrons.

Webb detected that light only faintly this time.

Ford said the next step is to compare these observations with simulations of how the gas evolves over longer stretches of time.

The abundances measured here are meant to go into those runs.

The full study was published in the journal The Astronomical Journal.
